items.title: Build ROS 2 Lyrical with Bazel: new ROS Central Registry release and a call for a working group

Maintenance of the mentioned tools is already quite challenging (I’m not directly involved, but based on observations). Wouldn’t all effort not going towards the established tools essentially complicate that even further? Less potential contributors, less interactions, less users, etc. If someone is happily using this new alternative, why bother ‘caring’ about anything else? Or do we assume the target audience (ie: those that have expressed or are interested in Bazel) would not fall in the potential contributors pool anyway? clalancette November 4, 2026, 1:28pm 3 gavanderhoorn: Or do we assume the target audience (ie: those that have expressed or are interested in Bazel) would not fall in the potential contributors pool anyway? My (very biased) observation is that this is indeed the case. Bazel is very compelling for a number of reasons if you have a large group of developers, the infrastructure team to support them, and a monorepo. And that set of people will probably contribute to the Bazel rules, and the Bazel rules only. But in my experience, Bazel is also immensely complex. So if you are a smaller team, or in academia, the complexity outweighs the advantages. For those type of teams, the existing tooling is an easier on-ramp, and I would expect these groups to contribute to the already-established tooling. Andrew_Symington November 4, 2026, 5:37pm 4 clalancette: My (very biased) observation is that this is indeed the case. Bazel is very compelling for a number of reasons if you have a large group of developers, the infrastructure team to support them, and a monorepo. I think a lot of this used to be true. With the creation of bzlmod, it has become much easier to federate code development and distribute maintenance responsibility (take a look at the number of contributors to the BCR: Contributors to bazelbuild/bazel-central-registry · GitHub ). In 2026 “monorepo mandate” argument no longer holds up. Many of the sharp edges encountered with Bazel stem from its design philosophy, and there are reasons behind all of the choices. The big ones are, firstly, it enforces a concrete dependency chain – even between targets across module boundaries. This decouples build behavior from the execution environment. Secondly, it forces you to explicitly list all files generated in the build – you can’t simply execute_process and file(GLOB ...) like you would in CMake. This is a good thing because if the output set of files is produced nondeterministically, then they can’t be hashed properly and so you cannot cache any derived targets. Thirdly, it sandboxes your build from the host, so you cannot simply probe for features like “am I running an aarch64 processor”. While inconvenient, this decouples the build from your architecture, and enables sysroot-less cross-compilation with a single flag like --platform @llvm//platforms:linux_aarch64_gnu.2.39 . Traditionally, with colcon the install folder tends to be a dumping ground for assets – and a lot of the time we just get lucky about asset availability because we build the whole workspace before we try and run anything. As a though exercise, consider how many packages in ROS install launch files but don’t exec_depend on launch_ros (eg. image_proc , lifecycle etc.). Bazel’s runfile design choice symlinks on the declared dependencies into the execution sandbox, ensuring reproducible builds. So, adding a launch_ros_binary() target puts a dep on launch_ros , ensuring that it is built and available in the sandbox when the launch is run. clalancette: And that set of people will probably contribute to the Bazel rules, and the Bazel rules only. I’d push back on this a little. I think there’s appetite for deploying ROS in products and we’re all trying to minimize crashes and bugs. The ideal place to land fixes is upstream. Bazel modules preserve patches as part of their metadata, and I think it’s low effort to move these to the source origin. In fact, I plan to run through all patches I needed to stabilize desktop_full in Bazel and move them upstream to the rolling branches. Concretely, I used --jobs and --runs_per_test flags in Bazel to catch nondeterminism under load, which can help find race conditions, like this one (where the xacro command needs to complete before the simulator launches). Andrew_Symington November 4, 2026, 6:00pm 5 gavanderhoorn: Maintenance of the mentioned tools is already quite challenging (I’m not directly involved, but based on observations). Yes it is. But that is the nature of robotics, and the reason ROS is such a powerful ecosystem. Because, we share this maintenance burden through collective tools. We should not shy away from problems because they are complex. I believe we should remain open to new ideas and tools that can benefit our ecosystem, even if they feel uncomfortable or different. In its current form, Bazel support is implemented as an augmentation (the build files live in modules outside of the repos) and so the risk of adoption is very low. However, it does take considerable effort maintaining these Bazel build files, but agentic tooling has simplified this work considerably. With enough examples in place – I hand-ported the base code to Bazel – LLMs are pretty good at transforming diffs to CMakeLists.txt and setup.py files to Bazel build file updates. gavanderhoorn: Wouldn’t all effort not going towards the established tools essentially complicate that even further? Less potential contributors, less interactions, less users, etc. If someone is happily using this new alternative, why bother ‘caring’ about anything else? I think open source works because we each care about a specific aspect of the system that contributes to the whole. The group of Bazel developers care about fast and reproducible builds; the only thing worse than a hard bug is a hard bug that presents 1 our1500 runs, right? And a lot of the work that is put into making this happen can be pushed upstream to packages with zero destructive interference to the Colcon and Pixi builds. The nature of these fixes will be formalizing dependency chains, fixing sources of nondeterminism, etc. I would consider this a form of care, although perhaps just not along the build system axis. gavanderhoorn: Or do we assume the target audience (ie: those that have expressed or are interested in Bazel) would not fall in the potential contributors pool anyway? I don’t see ROS developers a resource pool, and maintenance as a resource allocation problem. I see Bazel support as an opportunity to onboard developers from industry to work on ROS. This framework is meant to be deployed across many different kinds of environments which may have different kinds of devices and drastically different use cases. As a result, there won’t be a one-size-fits-all set of features or behaviors for the modules. A factory environment may care about high throughput above all else, whereas an airport environment may care about robustness to human presence more than throughput. This can lead to preferring different traffic management algorithms for each environment, and those traffic management systems may have different behaviors, capabilities, and requirements. This will lead to significant complexity in understanding how to compose an Open-RMF system correctly, because now the user needs to ensure that all the modules they choose to use are compatible and are suitable for their use-case and environment. It also complicates integration and e2e testing since expectations will vary by the choice of module implementations. This month’s discussion will be about Behavior Declarations , a concept we’re introducing to Next Gen Open-RMF to allow module implementations to declare (e.g. through a manifest file) what their capabilities and behaviors are, in a formal, extensible way. This will help users validate that combinations of module implementations match their intended use cases. Moreover, we will use these declarations to auto-generate and/or configure expectations for integration tests and e2e tests for combinations of module implementations. items.title: Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity
items.summary: Learn how Google Antigravity and our Cheminformatics Skills accelerate drug discovery workflows, search compounds, and propose novel rigidified macrocycles.
items.articleText: November 3, 2026 Science Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity Zoi Tsangalidou, Ruijie (Kelly) Zhang, Sukhdeep Singh and Michael V. LeVine Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity Share Designing new medicines requires curating complex data from charts, figures and literature, training predictive models, and proposing candidate molecules to synthesize — a workflow that typically takes multiple days for a single iteration. Here we show how Google Antigravity , equipped with our new Cheminformatics Skills, accelerates drug discovery workflows. Using real-world lung cancer treatments, an agent searches through thousands of compounds, performs matched molecular pair analysis, and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in just an hour. Chemistry is one of science’s richest public records — spanning millions of structures across journal articles and vendor catalogs. It provides a common representation that links physics and mathematics to the life and environmental sciences. Molecules and their transformations are ubiquitous and shape the everyday world. Despite decades of progress in cheminformatics, chemists still spend too much time wrangling data, a process complicated by the fact that molecules can be represented in many ways: from text descriptions to images or data structures. The same molecule can appear as an IUPAC name in a paper, a Markush structure in a patent, or a structure-data file (SDF) in a catalog. Advanced cheminformatics systems must be able to unify these sources and deal with the many ways errors can arise in them. This task has no margin for error – alter a single atom or bond and you have described a different compound altogether, rendering a promising inhibitor or catalyst inert. To let scientists focus on hypotheses rather than data wrangling, we built a suite of Cheminformatics Skills for Google Antigravity , turning the surface into a collaborative science workbench with full access to local tooling for both computational chemists and experimental bench chemists. The skills also create a division of labour where the underlying language model handles workflow orchestration, database navigation and scientific reasoning, while deterministic chemistry tools execute molecular calculations. Grounded in RDKit , the foundational open source cheminformatics toolkit developed over two decades by a global community of contributors, alongside connectors to curated resources from ChEMBL and PubChem , the skills encode domain best practices directly into the agent’s workflow. Rigidifying a floppy molecule In this technical walkthrough, we highlight a classic medicinal chemistry technique to improve drug potency: rigidification. Drug molecules can be complex, often linking multiple substructures through rotatable bonds. Those bonds let the molecule twist into many 3D shapes (conformations), making it “floppy” in solution. To bind its target, however, a floppy molecule must lock into a single active shape. Losing that freedom of motion carries an entropic penalty, which weakens binding affinity and lowers potency. To solve this problem, medicinal chemists often rigidify molecules by adding new bonds. Two substructures linked by a single rotatable bond can twist into many conformations, but adding a second bond to tie them together sharply limits how they can move in three dimensional space. By placing that bond in the right spot, chemists can lock the molecule into the exact shape needed to bind its target. This strategy, often called “paying the entropic cost in advance”, can dramatically boost potency. Here, we will focus on a well-known case of successful rigidification. The drug crizotinib is a first-generation, small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used to treat certain forms of non-small cell lung carcinoma. In crizotinib, there are five major rotatable bonds. Lorlatinib is a third-generation, small-molecule TKI that resembles crizotinib, but has been cyclized at its end to reduce the effective number of rotatable bonds to zero, leading to higher potency among other effects. Your browser does not support the video tag. Collaborative Intelligence We will ask the agent to search through literature for these drugs and their analogues. With the Cheminformatics skills in Antigravity, the agent is able to extract molecules from these documents, associate them with the data reported, and prepare the compounds for downstream analysis. Within minutes, the agent retrieves thousands of compounds, filters out irrelevant molecules (such as buffers and solvents), and documents their sources in a report. The report also provides an initial analysis of the retrieved compound set: highlighting, for example, that the macrocycles are largely predicted to be brain-penetrant, an important property given that the target lung cancer frequently metastasizes to the brain. For deeper exploration, the agent launches an interactive viewer displaying the curated compounds, their associated data, and customizable scatter plots. For example, plotting potency against rotatable bonds, colored by macrocycle status, immediately reveals that macrocycles like lorlatinib tend to have fewer rotatable bonds and higher potency. Ultimately, we designed these skills to not only expand the agent’s chemistry capabilities, but also to make user-agent collaboration seamless. Your browser does not support the video tag. In the interactive viewer, scientists can browse every compound retrieved from the literature, click individual molecules to inspect their metadata, and plot relationships across the dataset. For example, plotting cellular potency versus rotatable bonds,colored by macrocycle status, clearly shows that the highest potency compounds are the most rigid. After downloading and curating all the data, the agent is able to perform more advanced analysis to support the work of a computational chemist. As a next step, we will perform matched molecular pair analysis, a technique used in medicinal chemistry to isolate the effects of small, discrete changes to a molecule, by comparing pairs of molecules that only differ by that change. The agent had also independently suggested this analysis, as we expect the dataset to include many informative pairs. We will also ask the agent to build a predictive model using its molecular machine learning capabilities. The matched molecular pair analysis (MMPA) compared many pairs of molecules that differ by whether or not they are cyclized. The results of the analysis show that cyclization reduces the number of rotatable bonds while generally increasing potency, as expected. The agent also built a large number of potency models using varying feature sets and model architectures, and validated them on a held-out set. The skills provide the agent with guidance on how to best build molecular machine learning models - for example, the agent will often use chronological splits, training on older compounds to predict newer ones, when this information is available, but can fall back to scaffold splits to better estimate generalizability. The agent benchmarks multiple machine learning architectures with differing feature sets across four different experimental read outs, using a scaffold split to better gauge out-of-distribution performance. A combination of statistical and visual outputs allow the scientist to assess model performance and then iterate with the agent. Finally, we ask the agent to design new, improved macrocycles based on its learnings and it recommends multiple reactions and synthesis routes involving different compounds. The agent can prepare these compounds for further analysis with AlphaFold or physics-based techniques like molecular dynamics simulation. The skill equips the agent with the tools required to manipulate and validate reactions, generate curved arrow electron pushing diagrams, and look up similar reactions from public databases. The agent generated some interesting designs using its own knowledge combined with the previously developed MMPA and potency prediction models, explained its medicinal chemistry rationale, and suggested potential syntheses routes consistent with documented procedures. It also used the models it trained in the previous turn to predict each design’s potency. The agent is able to reason about chemistry as it proposes new synthesis plans. Here the agent proposes a cyclization reaction, providing the scientist with electron-pushing diagrams to demonstrate the mechanism. Once we are done with our analysis, the results can be exported in various formats, ready to be loaded into many industry standard chemistry software packages. At the same time, it is also important to know what these tools cannot do. Sparse data, inter-lab assay noise, and narrow dynamic ranges limit the predictive precision of even the most powerful models; computational designs are testable hypotheses, not finished drugs. With the Cheminformatics Skills in Antigravity, a drug discovery scientist can generate more strongly-supported design hypotheses faster, but every proposed design must be synthesized and validated experimentally. The speed at which researchers can make meaningful scientific decisions is accelerating. Not long ago, the workflow demonstrated here would have taken multiple days and required significant computational expertise. Using Antigravity as a science workbench allows both computational and experimental chemists to accelerate their workflows and focus on the questions that really matter. items.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
items.articleText: Recursive Self-Improvement via AI for Chip Design & Chip Design for AI - Ricursive Intelligence Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model. To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains. Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4). Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , and OpenRouter . Fireworks goes live later today. Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million . In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone. In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding , as estimated to the best of our knowledge.¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run. Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics. Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling , score centering , and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved. The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA. A Co-Designed Model Architecture Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization. Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping , gated attention , global NoPE , and value residuals . Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments. Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder , from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention . Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC ) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals . In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code. Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale. Conclusion We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier. We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors. At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If you’re interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers . ¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain. © 2026 Ricursive Intelligence, Inc.

## Verify Docker Image Signature

All LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/). This release is signed with the key introduced in [commit `e82a3c6`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/e82a3c646908ba0a6ee0beddc4310d7a6cac4065).

**Verify using the pinned commit hash (recommended):**

A commit hash is cryptographically immutable, so this is the strongest way to ensure you are using the published signing key:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/e82a3c646908ba0a6ee0beddc4310d7a6cac4065/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.108.0
```

**Verify using the release tag (convenience):**

Tags are protected in this repository and resolve to the same key. This option is easier to read but relies on tag protection rules:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.108.0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.108.0
```

Expected output:

```
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```

items.articleText: Robotics News Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor? Flying delivery robots prompt concern about noise, safety, and more David Berreby 5h 5 min read Is delivery of small objects in minutes worth the near-constant buzzing? Cheng Xin/Getty Images Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones . Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries. Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet )). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower. The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone. Delivery Drone Concerns Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility : “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.” As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies—including Alphabet’s Wing Aviation , Amazon Prime Air , Doordash Air , JD Logistics , Manna Aero , Matternet , Meituan , Zipline , and more, say their flying robots are quiet , safe , and unobtrusive . Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai , while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China . In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027 . And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026. A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot. Wing Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison , a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation , who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.” Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa . Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors . The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone. Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States , including suburban Detroit ; Richardson, Texas ; Glendale, Ariz .; East Cobb, Ga .; Maplewood, Mo .; and Westborough, Mass . The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely. An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia , shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament . In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped [its] engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms , and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens. Communities Take Action Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there. In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “overwhelmingly positive ,” and Zipline has encouraged at least one local official to refer to drone delivery as a “totally normal part of life.” Wing’s drone is smaller and lighter than some other delivery drones. Wing But fundamental concerns remain. “There are safety, noise, and visual-pollution issues with all these platforms,” Ison says, noting that it’s important not to lump all drone technologies together. For example, concerns about accidents are more relevant to Amazon’s MK-30 drone, which weighs almost 36 kilograms (80 pounds) , than to Wing’s largest drone, which weighs less than 11 kilograms (25 pounds) with its payload included . Another safety consideration: Wing and Zipline , he notes, lower their packages to the ground via a tether, which leaves the craft higher in the air than Amazon’s , which must get low enough to drop its load without damage. And Ison expects continuing disputes about noise. This is because U.S. law is not settled on people’s rights to airspace just above their property. “Maybe someone says, ‘You can’t fly over my house’ or ‘I want you to pay me to fly over my house,’ ” Ison says. “That is a murky area that is going to have to be worked out in court.” For now, in the Baton Rouge neighborhood where the LeComptes, Fugler, and Boone live, the skies have calmed. Their councilman says Amazon Prime Air has responded to the outcry by rerouting 70 percent of drone flights elsewhere, although since the drones are not allowed to fly over highways, that likely means other residential neighborhoods. As of late October, LeCompte says she is now seeing, “two or three a day” over their home, although on a trip to the bank a few miles away, she counted eight in 20 minutes. “Sorry for those folks, but I thank Amazon for clearing our sky.” From Your Site Articles U.S. Commercial Drone Delivery Comes Closer › The Way to Make Delivery Drones Work Is Using...Trucks? › When Drone Delivery Makes Sense › The Economics of Drone Delivery › Related Articles Around the Web UK aviation regulator warns of noise nuisance from drone deliveries and inspections - Dronewatch Europe › Amazon drone delivery test community complains about constant noise | Mashable › Drone technology: Start-ups look for ways to make quieter drones › drones Amazon Robotics delivery drones {"imageShortcodeIds":[]} David Berreby AI News How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses 03 Nov 2026 5 min read AI Consumer Electronics Sponsored Article Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream 29 Oct 2026 5 min read Computing News The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell 02 Nov 2026 4 min read Robotics Magazine Feature November 2026 Humanoid Robots The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build Robotics News This Disembodied Hand Is All the Robot You Need Consumer Electronics News Europe’s Circuit4EU Initiative Targets Rare Earths From E-Waste

items.articleText: The Robot Report tracks startups throughout the year, and our second annual Startup Radar spotlights some of the most interesting new companies developing commercial robotics and related technologies. From industrial automation and drones to humanoid robots, 2026 has been a year of innovation in the face of persistent labor shortages and geopolitical challenges. To qualify, organizations must be no more than five years old and must be working on enabling technologies, new full systems, or novel business approaches. The free download notes their application, headcount, and total funding raised to date. This year, we received a significant number of submissions around software, which is no surprise given the recent wave of interest and investment in data, simulation, and next-generation AI models. They promise to make robots more autonomous, combining the ability to perceive, understand, act, and improve. The 2026 Robotics Startup Radar features 60 companies working to serve a range of industries, from manufacturing and supply chain/warehousing to agriculture, defense, healthcare, and more. They are based in more than a dozen countries, and several have already successfully raised millions of dollars. What makes a successful robotics, automation, and AI startup? Such companies offer a strong technical foundation, teams with vision and experience, some business savvy, and key partnerships with industry stakeholders. While not every startup will scale or have an exit or an acquisition, understanding the target market is a key first step. The Robot Report will continue to cover and share financial news and success stories from this competitive space. As startups look to incubators and grants for support, investors and analysts are always looking for the next big thing and the right mix of technologies to continue expanding automation worldwide. Note that the call for The Robot Report (TRR) 50 Robotics Innovation Awards, to be presented at the Robotics Summit & Expo in Boston on June 2 and 3, 2027, is already open . items.title: How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot
items.summary: When designing the robot, GlobalLogic said it didn't want to just quickly design a robot for one use case or environment. The post How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: GlobalLogic developed the UV disinfection robot with Haystack Robotics. | Source: GlobalLogic In hospitals, hygiene is critical. But the cleaning process, which is time-intensive and difficult to scale, remains manual work. This often means the process is also inconsistent. Healthcare facilities are under pressure to care for more patients with fewer resources. These challenges are why the Silicon & Embedded division at GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics engineer a mobile robot to handle disinfection. The project started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when disinfection became a critical use case for robots. “Obviously, this was a big use case at that point of time, in terms of being able to sanitize hospitals and care facilities,” Kunaal Mahanti, physical AI lead at GlobalLogic, told The Robot Report . “So [Haystack ] came up with this concept of being able to do disinfection better.” “While there were disinfections which are happening manually, it wasn’t really good coverage,” he added. “We were really the engineering and collaboration partner there to see how we can take this concept and make it.” The result is an autonomous mobile robot (AMR ) that combines real-time perception, edge-based intelligence, and navigation to deliver hospital-grade UV disinfection with minimal human intervention. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company said it can operate safety alongside people, interpret its surroundings, and adapt to changes in its environment. GlobalLogic aims to create a scalable platform When designing its robot, Mahanti said GlobalLogic didn’t want to just quickly design a system for one use case or environment. “We wanted to make it an expandable platform,” he explained. “The idea was that you can look at, for example, the track part of it, which is the thing that is carrying the robot, independent of what it is carrying, which is the UV. Architecturally, you keep them separated so that we can mount other things at a later date.” “It went from a concept to what would be an architectural foundation, so that it’s not just that one product,” said Mahanti. “It actually becomes a class of solutions that we can build for the same industry segment.” While GlobalLogic hasn’t done many other deployments in hospitals , Mahanti did say the company used some of the base components of the UV robot for other projects. “When you look at the platform that moves, there are things that have come out from there in terms of the control of the motors,” he said. “Then we use ROS to do the programming and the sensor fusion part, that is reusable, and we’ve used that. So, if not necessarily the same device, but that architecture broadly.” Navigating the challenges that come with hospitals Healthcare facilities are crowded, chaotic, and involve many closed-off spaces, making them difficult for robots to work in. “The known part was that, obviously, you have to interact with humans. The unknown part is that there are doors, there are things that need to be opened, and you can’t always just barge in,” Mahanti said. This is different from more common use cases for mobile robots in warehousing or manufacturing, which typically involve open-spaces that are easy to navigate “There are two modes that we ended up building for [the robots],” noted Mahanti. “Essentially, one was this autonomous mode, where it would navigate and find the right room. The other was a ‘follow me’ mode, in which case it would follow a caregiver or a nurse.” This means the caregiver can open doors and ensure spaces are ready for the robot to enter. It also means a patient wouldn’t be blindsided by a robot entering their room, for example. However, designing an AMR that can work in these complex spaces has created benefits in other parts of GlobalLogic’s business. With a much higher bar for safety, the company could apply the platform to other industries. “The other learning is just being able to be in an environment where you cannot be loud, for example, when we are designing the motors or looking at what we need to put in [the robot],” said Mahanti. “Those things are specific to this industry, but then dealing with that has helped us build machines with higher fidelity elsewhere, where it is not necessarily a given, but it’s a good thing to have. Why wouldn’t you want to have a nice quiet thing that doesn’t interfere with the rest of the environment?” What’s holding back robotic adoption in hospitals? While more robots are making their way into hospitals, most people cannot yet walk into their local hospitals and find robots roaming the halls. This is still an emerging area for robotics, so what challenges still exist? Mahanti said three things come to mind. The first is cost. “There needs to be an ROI,” he replied. “For example, if you look at this use case during COVID, at that point of time, you needed less people in the hospitals. You needed to be safe. It was a big issue. So that ROI was justifiable.” Second is compliance with medical standards , which becomes much trickier when deploying robots that will interact with the public and patients. Third is the perception of robots. Mahanti acknowledged that hospital staffers don’t want a big, bulky robot taking up space in busy corridors and elevators. Prem Balasubramanian, chief technology officer of GlobalLogic, said that safely integrating into hospital workflows is also challenging. “There are clearly safety concerns, from multiple angles. Navigating in a very human-crowded situation is not easy,” he said. “For a disinfectant use case, if a robot waits for people to keep moving and then slowly moves, you’re okay. But if you’re using it for anything else, like if a doctor calls and you have to get something fast to help a patient or bring some stuff, a robot could get stuck because it sees people moving and it can’t move.” The hospital is difficult on its own, and it’s made even more difficult when you consider how made-for-humans they are, said Balasubramanian. For example, a robot might be able to navigate an emergency room in a perfect condition with no obstacles, but the addition of patients who constantly moving or being moved and staffers running around to solve critical issues make navigation much more challenging. “The entire workflow within a hospital is built for humans. You can’t just fit a robot in thinking it’s a human. So, there is work to be done in converting some of the workflow, the spaces, everything,” Balasubramanian said. Submit your innovation now! items.title: LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action
items.summary: LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation. The post LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action appeared first on The Robot Report .
items.articleText: LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation. In an evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6, it achieved 36.0% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those target tasks. The model combines large-scale human video, glove-recorded hand motion and embodiment alignment to transfer human manipulation experience to robots. Liber-0 achieves 36.0% overall success in a zero-shot evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6. LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a world action model (WAM) pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. The Beijing-based startup said the model combines human video with glove-recorded motion and embodiment-conditioned learning to transfer human manipulation experience to robots. A central test of Liber-0’s generalization is whether it can perform target tasks without robot demonstrations collected specifically for them. LiberAI evaluated the model on a separate suite of 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks, distinct from its internal scaling benchmarks: 20 pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, 20 non-PnP manipulation tasks, and 20 challenging non-PnP and long-horizon tasks. Examples from the suite include placing a pen in a pencil case, pushing a drawer closed, and a longer sequence in which a pen is placed in a pouch and the pouch is stored in a drawer. LiberAI reported task success rates of 63.5% on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on non-pick-and-place manipulation tasks and 10.5% on challenging non-pick-and-place and long-horizon tasks, with an overall success rate of 36.0% across 600 trials. Here, zero-shot means the evaluated checkpoint was not trained on robot demonstrations collected specifically for these target tasks; pretraining still included robot data. Why learn from people? Robot manipulation has traditionally relied heavily on demonstrations recorded on a specific robot for a specific task, usually by a human operator teleoperating the machine. That data closely matches deployment, but collecting it can be slow and expensive, particularly when new tasks or robot platforms require additional demonstrations. Human activity is far more abundant, and much of it is already on video. The obstacle, according to LiberAI, is that human video does not translate directly into robot commands. Cameras sit in different places, hand poses estimated from video are noisy, and human bodies move differently from robots. Liber-0 connects human experience with robot action in three ways. First, LiberSense Glove, LiberAI’s data-collection system, directly records hand movements, helping link human video to the motions behind it. Second, LiberAI’s robot platform uses camera views and hand, wrist and waist movements that more closely match those of humans, making skills easier to transfer. Third, a Unified Embodiment Representation gives the model information about body shape and joint movement, so it can adapt actions to the body performing them. Liber-0 jointly predicts future video frames and actions. This lets it learn from ordinary videos without action labels alongside glove and robot recordings that include measured motion. Human-to-robot transfer. Conceptual illustration of how action-grounded human recordings and visual and kinematic alignment support transfer to LEO. Learning actions that robot data lacked Glove data can also introduce behaviors missing from a policy’s robot data. LiberAI trained policies whose robot demonstrations covered only pick-and-place, while glove demonstrations included actions such as folding, pressing and opening. Performance was measured as a progress score, a 0 to 100 measure that credits partial completion, across four pick-and-place and six non-PnP tasks. With robot data alone, the non-PnP progress score was 2.2. Adding glove recordings of those actions raised it to 47.5, and to 54.6 when the glove set also included pick-and-place, close to the 56.3 scored by a policy trained on robot demonstrations of every action. This controlled experiment is separate from the 60-task suite: the actions appeared in the glove demonstrations but not in the policies’ robot demonstrations. A quarter of the robot data A separate experiment examines whether glove recordings can reduce the need for robot demonstrations. In an eight-task evaluation on LiberAI’s robot platform, where the full robot and glove pools contained equal numbers of demonstrations, a policy trained on 25% of the robot pool plus 100% of the glove pool reached a progress score of 75.6. A policy trained on 100% of the robot pool scored 72.8. In that setting, glove recordings delivered comparable performance with 75% fewer robot demonstrations. The saving applies to robot demonstrations specifically, as the mixed policy still drew on the full glove pool. Because glove collection does not require a robot at each site, LiberAI says experience can be gathered from more people, in more places, and potentially at lower cost. Evaluating the pretrained model directly On LiberAI’s internal benchmarks, the pretrained checkpoint achieved progress scores of 81.4 on pick-and-place and 72.3 on non-PnP tasks when evaluated directly. Robot post-training added 2.2 and 1.5 points, to 83.6 and 73.8. LiberAI said the small gain indicates the pretrained model already captures much of the capability needed for the evaluated tasks. LiberAI has developed an interactive simulation in which users can upload their own objects and watch Liber-0 manipulate them in a virtual environment. The simulation demonstrates object-level generalization: that version of the model was post-trained on 100 hours of simulated teleoperation data and receives no further object-specific training. “Human video shows what people do, but not exactly how their hands move or how that movement fits a different body,” said Songming Liu, founder and CEO of LiberAI. “Grounding that experience in measured motion and aligning it with the robot’s body is what turns it into robot capability.” Introducing Liber-0, our World Action Model for zero-shot robot manipulation—including dexterous, multi-step tasks. Across 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6 and 600 trials, Liber-0 achieved 36% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those tasks: • Pick-and-place: 63.5% • Other manipulation tasks: 34.0% • Challenging multi-step tasks: 10.5% Zero-shot capability extends beyond individual actions to coordinated sequences. Pretrained on 2.2M+ hours of human experience, Liber-0 jointly predicts future observations and actions to turn human experience into robot skills. Technical blog: https://t.co/X5NMTjsr8r — LiberAI (@liberai_robot) November 4, 2026 What’s next for LiberAI LiberAI noted that LiberSense Glove currently records hand poses and trajectories but not contact or force, which matter for insertion, fastening and handling soft materials. Tactile and force sensing, alongside data collection across a wider range of homes, remain future research directions. Watch Liber-0 in action and explore the full evaluation on LiberAI . For collaboration on models, robotics, LiberSense Glove or other opportunities, contact the LiberAI team via the website. Sponsored content by LiberAI Tell Us What You Think! entries.title: Google DeepMind, Google Antigravity용 Cheminformatics Skills 공개

The RCR is a community Bazel build for ROS, from Lyrical onward. It’s designed to complement colcon, pixi and other build tools, not replace them . It’s still a proof of concept, and community adoption and involvement will decide its future. Why Bazel As teams and projects grow, there are good reasons to consider Bazel for build orchestration. Andrew covers them in the ROSCon 2026 talk . Several open-source Bazel rule sets for ROS already exist, and some companies maintain their own private ones. The RCR is an effort to consolidate this work. It uses Bazel modules for federation, and hermetic C++, Python and Rust toolchains for determinism. What’s in this release Packages: a lot of rosdistro is working, including message pipelines, nodes, components, launch, rviz2, MoveIt, Nav2 and Gazebo Platforms: Linux (aarch64 and x86_64) and macOS (aarch64) GUIs: Qt 6 built from source Build cache: Intrinsic provides a read-only GCS-backed cache, which CI warms on every commit to main , to keep builds fast by default. If you’d rather build everything locally, edit .bazelrc before building. Try it Example repo to get started: GitHub - asymingt/rcr-example: Repo with simple examples showcasing features of the ROS Central Registry (RCR) · GitHub Package index: https://bazel.ros.org Tooling and modules (open PRs here): GitHub - openrobotics/ros-central-registry: ROS packages as Bazel modules · GitHub Package index source: GitHub - openrobotics/rcr-frontend: Website for the ROS Central Registry · GitHub Get involved There are likely still bugs, and patching, rollup and release tooling is in place to fix them. To contribute a fix, read the docs in the ros-central-registry repo, or point your agentic coding tool at AGENTS.md and the .agent/skills folder. They explain how to provision a workspace, vendor a package, fix the source and roll up a patch. CI checks that no breaking changes are introduced. Andrew intends to start a working group to coordinate developers and maintainers. If you’re interested in joining, send @Andrew_Symington a DM to be added to the list. This work builds on a lot of previous effort, notably by the Bazel team and by Milan Vukov through rules_ros2 . Andrew specifically recognizes Milan’s design for the IDL aspects that traverse message dependency chains to generate language bindings, one of the hardest parts to get right. Thanks, Andrew, for all this work! Maintenance of the mentioned tools is already quite challenging (I’m not directly involved, but based on observations). Wouldn’t all effort not going towards the established tools essentially complicate that even further? Less potential contributors, less interactions, less users, etc. If someone is happily using this new alternative, why bother ‘caring’ about anything else? And that set of people will probably contribute to the Bazel rules, and the Bazel rules only. But in my experience, Bazel is also immensely complex. So if you are a smaller team, or in academia, the complexity outweighs the advantages. In 2026 “monorepo mandate” argument no longer holds up. Many of the sharp edges encountered with Bazel stem from its design philosophy, and there are reasons behind all of the choices. The big ones are, firstly, it enforces a concrete dependency chain – even between targets across module boundaries. This decouples build behavior from the execution environment. Secondly, it forces you to explicitly list all files generated in the build – you can’t simply execute_process and file(GLOB ...) like you would in CMake. This is a good thing because if the output set of files is produced nondeterministically, then they can’t be hashed properly and so you cannot cache any derived targets. Thirdly, it sandboxes your build from the host, so you cannot simply probe for features like “am I running an aarch64 processor”. While inconvenient, this decouples the build from your architecture, and enables sysroot-less cross-compilation with a single flag like --platform @llvm//platforms:linux_aarch64_gnu.2.39 . Traditionally, with colcon the install folder tends to be a dumping ground for assets – and a lot of the time we just get lucky about asset availability because we build the whole workspace before we try and run anything. As a though exercise, consider how many packages in ROS install launch files but don’t exec_depend on launch_ros (eg. image_proc , lifecycle etc.). Bazel’s runfile design choice symlinks on the declared dependencies into the execution sandbox, ensuring reproducible builds. So, adding a launch_ros_binary() target puts a dep on launch_ros , ensuring that it is built and available in the sandbox when the launch is run. clalancette: And that set of people will probably contribute to the Bazel rules, and the Bazel rules only. I’d push back on this a little. I think there’s appetite for deploying ROS in products and we’re all trying to minimize crashes and bugs. The ideal place to land fixes is upstream. Bazel modules preserve patches as part of their metadata, and I think it’s low effort to move these to the source origin. In fact, I plan to run through all patches I needed to stabilize desktop_full in Bazel and move them upstream to the rolling branches. Concretely, I used --jobs and --runs_per_test flags in Bazel to catch nondeterminism under load, which can help find race conditions, like this one (where the xacro command needs to complete before the simulator launches). Andrew_Symington November 4, 2026, 6:00pm 5 gavanderhoorn: Maintenance of the mentioned tools is already quite challenging (I’m not directly involved, but based on observations). Yes it is. But that is the nature of robotics, and the reason ROS is such a powerful ecosystem. Because, we share this maintenance burden through collective tools. We should not shy away from problems because they are complex. I believe we should remain open to new ideas and tools that can benefit our ecosystem, even if they feel uncomfortable or different. In its current form, Bazel support is implemented as an augmentation (the build files live in modules outside of the repos) and so the risk of adoption is very low. However, it does take considerable effort maintaining these Bazel build files, but agentic tooling has simplified this work considerably. With enough examples in place – I hand-ported the base code to Bazel – LLMs are pretty good at transforming diffs to CMakeLists.txt and setup.py files to Bazel build file updates. gavanderhoorn: Wouldn’t all effort not going towards the established tools essentially complicate that even further? Less potential contributors, less interactions, less users, etc. If someone is happily using this new alternative, why bother ‘caring’ about anything else? I think open source works because we each care about a specific aspect of the system that contributes to the whole. The group of Bazel developers care about fast and reproducible builds; the only thing worse than a hard bug is a hard bug that presents 1 our1500 runs, right? And a lot of the work that is put into making this happen can be pushed upstream to packages with zero destructive interference to the Colcon and Pixi builds. The nature of these fixes will be formalizing dependency chains, fixing sources of nondeterminism, etc. I would consider this a form of care, although perhaps just not along the build system axis. gavanderhoorn: Or do we assume the target audience (ie: those that have expressed or are interested in Bazel) would not fall in the potential contributors pool anyway? I don’t see ROS developers a resource pool, and maintenance as a resource allocation problem. I see Bazel support as an opportunity to onboard developers from industry to work on ROS. selectedItems.summary: Learn how Google Antigravity and our Cheminformatics Skills accelerate drug discovery workflows, search compounds, and propose novel rigidified macrocycles.
selectedItems.articleText: November 3, 2026 Science Agentic cheminformatics with Google Antigravity Zoi Tsangalidou, Ruijie (Kelly) Zhang, Sukhdeep Singh and Michael V. LeVine Explore scientific workflows in Google Antigravity Share Designing new medicines requires curating complex data from charts, figures and literature, training predictive models, and proposing candidate molecules to synthesize — a workflow that typically takes multiple days for a single iteration. Here we show how Google Antigravity , equipped with our new Cheminformatics Skills, accelerates drug discovery workflows. Using real-world lung cancer treatments, an agent searches through thousands of compounds, performs matched molecular pair analysis, and proposes novel rigidified macrocycles with synthetic routes in just an hour. Chemistry is one of science’s richest public records — spanning millions of structures across journal articles and vendor catalogs. It provides a common representation that links physics and mathematics to the life and environmental sciences. Molecules and their transformations are ubiquitous and shape the everyday world. Despite decades of progress in cheminformatics, chemists still spend too much time wrangling data, a process complicated by the fact that molecules can be represented in many ways: from text descriptions to images or data structures. The same molecule can appear as an IUPAC name in a paper, a Markush structure in a patent, or a structure-data file (SDF) in a catalog. Advanced cheminformatics systems must be able to unify these sources and deal with the many ways errors can arise in them. This task has no margin for error – alter a single atom or bond and you have described a different compound altogether, rendering a promising inhibitor or catalyst inert. To let scientists focus on hypotheses rather than data wrangling, we built a suite of Cheminformatics Skills for Google Antigravity , turning the surface into a collaborative science workbench with full access to local tooling for both computational chemists and experimental bench chemists. The skills also create a division of labour where the underlying language model handles workflow orchestration, database navigation and scientific reasoning, while deterministic chemistry tools execute molecular calculations. Grounded in RDKit , the foundational open source cheminformatics toolkit developed over two decades by a global community of contributors, alongside connectors to curated resources from ChEMBL and PubChem , the skills encode domain best practices directly into the agent’s workflow. Rigidifying a floppy molecule In this technical walkthrough, we highlight a classic medicinal chemistry technique to improve drug potency: rigidification. Drug molecules can be complex, often linking multiple substructures through rotatable bonds. Those bonds let the molecule twist into many 3D shapes (conformations), making it “floppy” in solution. To bind its target, however, a floppy molecule must lock into a single active shape. Losing that freedom of motion carries an entropic penalty, which weakens binding affinity and lowers potency. To solve this problem, medicinal chemists often rigidify molecules by adding new bonds. Two substructures linked by a single rotatable bond can twist into many conformations, but adding a second bond to tie them together sharply limits how they can move in three dimensional space. By placing that bond in the right spot, chemists can lock the molecule into the exact shape needed to bind its target. This strategy, often called “paying the entropic cost in advance”, can dramatically boost potency. Here, we will focus on a well-known case of successful rigidification. The drug crizotinib is a first-generation, small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) used to treat certain forms of non-small cell lung carcinoma. In crizotinib, there are five major rotatable bonds. Lorlatinib is a third-generation, small-molecule TKI that resembles crizotinib, but has been cyclized at its end to reduce the effective number of rotatable bonds to zero, leading to higher potency among other effects. Your browser does not support the video tag. Collaborative Intelligence We will ask the agent to search through literature for these drugs and their analogues. With the Cheminformatics skills in Antigravity, the agent is able to extract molecules from these documents, associate them with the data reported, and prepare the compounds for downstream analysis. Within minutes, the agent retrieves thousands of compounds, filters out irrelevant molecules (such as buffers and solvents), and documents their sources in a report. The report also provides an initial analysis of the retrieved compound set: highlighting, for example, that the macrocycles are largely predicted to be brain-penetrant, an important property given that the target lung cancer frequently metastasizes to the brain. For deeper exploration, the agent launches an interactive viewer displaying the curated compounds, their associated data, and customizable scatter plots. For example, plotting potency against rotatable bonds, colored by macrocycle status, immediately reveals that macrocycles like lorlatinib tend to have fewer rotatable bonds and higher potency. Ultimately, we designed these skills to not only expand the agent’s chemistry capabilities, but also to make user-agent collaboration seamless. Your browser does not support the video tag. In the interactive viewer, scientists can browse every compound retrieved from the literature, click individual molecules to inspect their metadata, and plot relationships across the dataset. For example, plotting cellular potency versus rotatable bonds,colored by macrocycle status, clearly shows that the highest potency compounds are the most rigid. After downloading and curating all the data, the agent is able to perform more advanced analysis to support the work of a computational chemist. As a next step, we will perform matched molecular pair analysis, a technique used in medicinal chemistry to isolate the effects of small, discrete changes to a molecule, by comparing pairs of molecules that only differ by that change. The agent had also independently suggested this analysis, as we expect the dataset to include many informative pairs. We will also ask the agent to build a predictive model using its molecular machine learning capabilities. The matched molecular pair analysis (MMPA) compared many pairs of molecules that differ by whether or not they are cyclized. The results of the analysis show that cyclization reduces the number of rotatable bonds while generally increasing potency, as expected. The agent also built a large number of potency models using varying feature sets and model architectures, and validated them on a held-out set. The skills provide the agent with guidance on how to best build molecular machine learning models - for example, the agent will often use chronological splits, training on older compounds to predict newer ones, when this information is available, but can fall back to scaffold splits to better estimate generalizability. The agent benchmarks multiple machine learning architectures with differing feature sets across four different experimental read outs, using a scaffold split to better gauge out-of-distribution performance. A combination of statistical and visual outputs allow the scientist to assess model performance and then iterate with the agent. Finally, we ask the agent to design new, improved macrocycles based on its learnings and it recommends multiple reactions and synthesis routes involving different compounds. The agent can prepare these compounds for further analysis with AlphaFold or physics-based techniques like molecular dynamics simulation. The skill equips the agent with the tools required to manipulate and validate reactions, generate curved arrow electron pushing diagrams, and look up similar reactions from public databases. The agent generated some interesting designs using its own knowledge combined with the previously developed MMPA and potency prediction models, explained its medicinal chemistry rationale, and suggested potential syntheses routes consistent with documented procedures. It also used the models it trained in the previous turn to predict each design’s potency. The agent is able to reason about chemistry as it proposes new synthesis plans. Here the agent proposes a cyclization reaction, providing the scientist with electron-pushing diagrams to demonstrate the mechanism. Once we are done with our analysis, the results can be exported in various formats, ready to be loaded into many industry standard chemistry software packages. At the same time, it is also important to know what these tools cannot do. Sparse data, inter-lab assay noise, and narrow dynamic ranges limit the predictive precision of even the most powerful models; computational designs are testable hypotheses, not finished drugs. With the Cheminformatics Skills in Antigravity, a drug discovery scientist can generate more strongly-supported design hypotheses faster, but every proposed design must be synthesized and validated experimentally. The speed at which researchers can make meaningful scientific decisions is accelerating. Not long ago, the workflow demonstrated here would have taken multiple days and required significant computational expertise. Using Antigravity as a science workbench allows both computational and experimental chemists to accelerate their workflows and focus on the questions that really matter. Acknowledgements The cheminformatics skills are available on Google Antigravity today. Download the Antigravity App and install the Science plugin to start using these skills. Explore Science use cases here . You can also get started with cheminformatics on Antigravity today as an Enterprise user, by choosing “Use Business Account” and logging into the app with your Google Cloud credentials. To further advance the pace of research, we’re offering 10,000 scientists the highest usage tier in Google Antigravity free of charge for 6 months (onboarded on a rolling basis), subject to eligibility, capacity, and selection. Applications are now open . We would like to acknowledge the contributions of the following team members: Filip Radlinski, Artem Sobolev, Victoria Johnston, Hannah Kiely-Collins, Zachary Wu, Jue Wang, Jack Dunger, Adriana Fernandez Lara, Ngân Vũ, Doug Fritz, Yunhan Xu, Sebastian Nowozin, Pushmeet Kohli. selectedItems.title: Ripple-65B Preview: U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding
selectedItems.articleText: Recursive Self-Improvement via AI for Chip Design & Chip Design for AI - Ricursive Intelligence Introducing Ripple-65B Preview, a Frontier Open-Weight Model Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Achieving U.S. Open-Weight SOTA on Agentic Coding Ricursive Intelligence is a full-stack artificial intelligence lab building self-improving systems by co-optimizing hardware, software, and model. To power our chip design platform, we trained a language model from scratch that sets a new U.S. open-weight SOTA on agentic coding. We optimized the model architecture for our training and serving platforms, driving substantial efficiency gains. Today, we release Ripple-65B Preview , a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model that powers our AI chip design platform. The model is pretrained on 12 trillion tokens with support for up to 1M context length. Ripple-65B Preview delivers strong results on agentic coding, achieving U.S. open-weight state-of-the-art (80.52) on TerminalBench 2.1 and surpassing significantly larger US open-weight models such as Reflection Beam 501B (80.1), Meta Muse Spark Open 816B (76.4), Thinking Machines Inkling 975B (63.8), and NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B (56.4). Ripple’s dense model architecture provides strong reasoning performance with low-latency token generation. The model’s small parameter envelope also enables it to run efficiently on local devices such as NVIDIA DGX Spark, which feature high compute FLOPs with low memory bandwidth relative to datacenter accelerators. Ripple-65B Preview is available on Hugging Face , Together AI , GMI Cloud , and OpenRouter . Fireworks goes live later today. Achieving U.S. Open-Weight Frontier at One-Tenth Cost LLM pretraining is legendarily expensive. In 2023, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that GPT-4 training costs exceeded $100 million . In the following year, Dario Amodei said that frontier AI models can cost up to $1 billion to train, projecting that costs would rise to $10-100B by 2026 to 2027 for pretraining alone. In contrast, we developed and trained Ripple-65B Preview for only $32M, which is one-tenth the cost of the previous open-weight SOTA on agentic coding , as estimated to the best of our knowledge.¹ Note that $32M is our full R&D cost starting from scratch, including pretraining ladder development, data mixing, evals, debugging, synthetic data generation, posttraining recipe development, and the final hero pretraining and posttraining run. Steep Ascent Reinforcement Learning Rather than investing in a brute-force RL climb, we carefully iterated on our SFT and RL recipes with a focus on compute efficiency. We opted not to buy any posttraining data, instead devising our own synthetic data pipelines, quality filtering, and coverage metrics. Our mixed RL recipe uses truncated importance sampling , score centering , and linear length penalty with high-quality long-horizon synthetic environments. The RL tasks are tuned for our model capabilities, and we continuously added harder tasks as the model improved. The end result was a steep RL climb from a strong initial SFT checkpoint. We reached a TerminalBench 2.1 score of 80.5 with only 1.4M rollouts, roughly 70x fewer rollouts than Reflection Beam, the prior SOTA. A Co-Designed Model Architecture Ripple-65B Preview’s architecture was designed to be trained and served efficiently on NVIDIA hardware. A key objective was to make design decisions which reduce pretraining and posttraining infrastructure complexity while still enabling strong reasoning and agentic performance. Therefore, we chose to train a modernized dense Transformer model rather than use Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) like other labs. This decision quickly paid off, and we were able to train a strong model from scratch while maintaining a solid MFU (40%) throughout pretraining and posttraining, even with simple sharding, no custom kernels, and no quantization. Ripple-65B Preview uses a thin-and-deep model aspect ratio, with a narrow d_model (5120) and 80 total layers. To improve reasoning performance, we overprovision the number of attention heads while increasing the SWA-to-global layer ratio and reducing SWA window size to compensate for the increased cost. In addition, we added FFN activation clipping , gated attention , global NoPE , and value residuals . Careful Model Laddering Led to Large Improvements We optimized Ripple’s pretraining recipe through a series of careful model laddering experiments. Our starting point was Olmo 3’s model ladder , from which we tested interventions at small scale with a focus on improving coding capabilities. Our v1.0 ladder implemented StepFun batch size and learning rate scaling laws, and v1.1 implemented our new ladder which smoothly scales architectural dimensions and model depth. Ladder v1.2 switched from the post-norm baseline to pre+post norm, which was neutral at small scale but showed improvements starting at 4B. Ladder v1.3 implemented sigmoid gated attention . Ladder v1.4 (2-stream mHC ) showed good results at smaller scale but did not improve at 4B scale, and was therefore rejected. Ladder v1.5 switched to global NoPE and added a final LR cooldown to zero, and ladder v1.6 added value residuals . In the final version, we switched to our custom pretraining dataset with substantially upsampled code. Together, the compounded changes improved compute efficiency on code as measured by dolma_stack CE by up to 16x at 4B model scale. In other words, our final Ripple model ladder can be used to achieve similar code performance to the Olmo 3 ladder with 16x less compute . Note that the slope of the Olmo 3 ladder baseline is shallower than ladder v1.0+, which shows that the compute efficiency improvement will increase with additional scale. Conclusion We built Ripple-65B Preview to begin closing the loop between models and the hardware that fuels them. An internal variant of this model powers our AI chip design platform, and we look forward to seeing the capabilities that emerge as we scale toward the frontier. We were fortunate to build on top of existing open-source contributions, including those from the Olmo team at the Allen Institute for AI (AI2), Prime Intellect, RadixArk, and NVIDIA. A strong open-source ecosystem is also self-improving, where contributors strengthen the ecosystem, which in turn draws more contributors. At Ricursive, we are selectively hiring exceptional researchers and engineers as we push the frontier of full-stack AI from model to silicon. If you’re interested, check out https://www.ricursive.com/careers . ¹ U.S. open-weight players like Reflection were reported to commit to $150M per month for compute at SpaceX Colossus to train their models. Reflection reported that Beam took 4 weeks to pretrain and 4 weeks to posttrain. © 2026 Ricursive Intelligence, Inc.

## Verify Docker Image Signature

All LiteLLM Docker images are signed with [cosign](https://docs.sigstore.dev/cosign/overview/). This release is signed with the key introduced in [commit `e82a3c6`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm/commit/e82a3c646908ba0a6ee0beddc4310d7a6cac4065).

**Verify using the pinned commit hash (recommended):**

A commit hash is cryptographically immutable, so this is the strongest way to ensure you are using the published signing key:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/e82a3c646908ba0a6ee0beddc4310d7a6cac4065/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.108.0
```

**Verify using the release tag (convenience):**

Tags are protected in this repository and resolve to the same key. This option is easier to read but relies on tag protection rules:

```bash
cosign verify \
  --key https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/v1.108.0/cosign.pub \
  ghcr.io/berriai/litellm:v1.108.0
```

Expected output:

```
The following checks were performed on each of these signatures:
  - The cosign claims were validated
  - The signatures were verified against the specified public key
```
