selectedItems.articleText: Robotics News Are Drone Ports the Next Annoying Tech Neighbor? Flying delivery robots prompt concern about noise, safety, and more David Berreby 5h 5 min read Is delivery of small objects in minutes worth the near-constant buzzing? Cheng Xin/Getty Images Rick and Marcia LeCompte loved to watch the Cooper’s hawks that frequented a sweet-gum tree in their yard in Baton Rouge, La. But this October, the hawks were gone. Marcia LeCompte is convinced the birds were scared away by the same flying robots that have been vexing the couple since early September. The noise had them spending less time outside in their garden, and even inside their home, they couldn’t escape the near-constant buzzing. Angry and feeling harassed, the LeComptes began to think about moving. The problem: delivery drones . Amazon’s MK30 delivery drones are large and must fly near the ground when making deliveries. Annabel Lee-Ellis/Press Association/AP Images Last August, Amazon Prime Air began flying its MK30 drones from a distribution center 3.2 kilometers (2 miles) from the LeComptes’ home. People in the neighborhood first noticed just a few of the drones, flying high (U.S. regulations authorize drones to fly at up to 120 meters (400 feet )). But a couple of weeks later, they felt as if drones were everywhere, and often flying much lower. The high-pitched whine of rotors was what bothered them the most, says Blake Fugler, who lives in the same neighborhood. It sounded as if a neighbor was constantly using a weed whacker for hours every day, he says. Acoustic research has found that the noise of drone rotors is more annoying than that of cars, airplanes, and other familiar background sounds. Once flights became frequent, the noise made people miserable. “Outside the house on a Saturday between 9 and 10 a.m., I counted a drone every 48 seconds,” says Fugler’s partner, Cristina Boone. Delivery Drone Concerns Neighbors had concerns about drones buzzing over playgrounds, schools, and services at the local cemetery; a drone that made a forced landing on the median of a busy highway; and the fact that drones are equipped with cameras. Then word spread about Amazon’s plans as reported in the FAA’s Environmental Assessment for the facility : “Operations would occur between 6 a.m. and 10:30 p.m., with 100 of the 1,000 daily delivery operations (10%) occurring during the period from 6 a.m. to 7 a.m. and 10 p.m. to 10:30 p.m.” As they quickly expand their operations around the world, delivery-drone companies—including Alphabet’s Wing Aviation , Amazon Prime Air , Doordash Air , JD Logistics , Manna Aero , Matternet , Meituan , Zipline , and more, say their flying robots are quiet , safe , and unobtrusive . Massive expansion is planned for the near future. In Asia, for example, Meituan launched its latest “low-altitude delivery network’’ in September in Shanghai , while JD continues to expand drone service in rural China . In the U.S., Zipline and Uber have announced a partnership with the goal of 1 million drone deliveries a day by the end of 2029. Wing aims to have 270 U.S. drone hubs operating by the end of 2027 . And Amazon Prime Air, which currently delivers in about 85 municipalities in the U.S., says it plans to serve 500 by the end of 2026. A Wing “nest” of delivery drones in a parking lot. Wing Yet as the companies aggressively scale up, “the public outreach piece has probably been more of an afterthought than it should have been,” says David Ison , a specialist in Emerging Aviation Technologies and Land Use Compatibility at the Washington State Department of Transportation , who has worked on the state’s drone-hub land-use guidelines. “I think what companies assumed is everybody would be cheering that they could get things delivered by drone in half an hour.” Companies tout drone delivery as a way to do good. Zipline has delivered blood plasma and vaccines in Africa . Material that Wing provided at public meetings in the Dallas Fort Worth area says its deliveries there have saved more than 1,000 tonnes of carbon that would have been emitted by delivery trucks. For businesses, drone delivery is supposed to offer faster service and reduce costs, although whether drones are actually less costly is a complex question that depends on a variety of interconnected factors . The commercial and philanthropic use cases make for an unusual sales pitch, notes Ison. “It’s a lot easier argument to make when you’re saying you’re delivering blood to an accident site than when you’re delivering a fidget toy.” But instead of being impressed, people troubled by drones say they feel they’re being pushed around by a distant corporation. “It’s the same way data centers strong-arm communities,” says Boone. Newly arrived drone launch sites have triggered similar fears from China to France to Australia to within many communities in the United States , including suburban Detroit ; Richardson, Texas ; Glendale, Ariz .; East Cobb, Ga .; Maplewood, Mo .; and Westborough, Mass . The response has sometimes been enough to shut down local drone operations completely. An early Wing trial in 2018 in suburban Canberra, Australia , shut down a few months later, after activists formed an opposition group and rallied support in Parliament . In response, the company “fundamentally reshaped [its] engineering priorities, flight operations, and community-engagement strategy,” says Jessie Poole-Strang, Wing’s communications lead. It redesigned its drones to reduce noise, changed flight-path algorithms , and now makes efforts to familiarize people with its robots before a facility opens. Communities Take Action Still, legal and political campaigns against drones continue to arise. On 28 September, 15 U.S. states and Harris County, Texas, sued the FAA to stop it from easing its environmental assessment rules for drone sites, which are key to local government control. In April, the Cobb County Board of Commissioners in Georgia denied a zoning request for a Wing drone facility there. In response to the Cobb County complaints, a Wing spokesperson said the company was hearing “positive feedback” from people in Cobb County. Similarly, Amazon representatives have said most feedback from customers about drone delivery is “overwhelmingly positive ,” and Zipline has encouraged at least one local official to refer to drone delivery as a “totally normal part of life.” Wing’s drone is smaller and lighter than some other delivery drones. Wing But fundamental concerns remain. “There are safety, noise, and visual-pollution issues with all these platforms,” Ison says, noting that it’s important not to lump all drone technologies together. For example, concerns about accidents are more relevant to Amazon’s MK-30 drone, which weighs almost 36 kilograms (80 pounds) , than to Wing’s largest drone, which weighs less than 11 kilograms (25 pounds) with its payload included . Another safety consideration: Wing and Zipline , he notes, lower their packages to the ground via a tether, which leaves the craft higher in the air than Amazon’s , which must get low enough to drop its load without damage. And Ison expects continuing disputes about noise. This is because U.S. law is not settled on people’s rights to airspace just above their property. “Maybe someone says, ‘You can’t fly over my house’ or ‘I want you to pay me to fly over my house,’ ” Ison says. “That is a murky area that is going to have to be worked out in court.” For now, in the Baton Rouge neighborhood where the LeComptes, Fugler, and Boone live, the skies have calmed. Their councilman says Amazon Prime Air has responded to the outcry by rerouting 70 percent of drone flights elsewhere, although since the drones are not allowed to fly over highways, that likely means other residential neighborhoods. As of late October, LeCompte says she is now seeing, “two or three a day” over their home, although on a trip to the bank a few miles away, she counted eight in 20 minutes. “Sorry for those folks, but I thank Amazon for clearing our sky.” From Your Site Articles U.S. Commercial Drone Delivery Comes Closer › The Way to Make Delivery Drones Work Is Using...Trucks? › When Drone Delivery Makes Sense › The Economics of Drone Delivery › Related Articles Around the Web UK aviation regulator warns of noise nuisance from drone deliveries and inspections - Dronewatch Europe › Amazon drone delivery test community complains about constant noise | Mashable › Drone technology: Start-ups look for ways to make quieter drones › drones Amazon Robotics delivery drones {"imageShortcodeIds":[]} David Berreby AI News How a Kenyan Startup Is Rethinking AI for Small Businesses 03 Nov 2026 5 min read AI Consumer Electronics Sponsored Article Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream 29 Oct 2026 5 min read Computing News The PHP2Shell Vulnerability Heralds Cybersecurity Hell 02 Nov 2026 4 min read Robotics Magazine Feature November 2026 Humanoid Robots The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build Robotics News This Disembodied Hand Is All the Robot You Need Consumer Electronics News Europe’s Circuit4EU Initiative Targets Rare Earths From E-Waste

selectedItems.title: How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot
selectedItems.summary: When designing the robot, GlobalLogic said it didn't want to just quickly design a robot for one use case or environment. The post How GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics build a UV disinfection robot appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: GlobalLogic developed the UV disinfection robot with Haystack Robotics. | Source: GlobalLogic In hospitals, hygiene is critical. But the cleaning process, which is time-intensive and difficult to scale, remains manual work. This often means the process is also inconsistent. Healthcare facilities are under pressure to care for more patients with fewer resources. These challenges are why the Silicon & Embedded division at GlobalLogic helped Haystack Robotics engineer a mobile robot to handle disinfection. The project started during the COVID-19 pandemic, when disinfection became a critical use case for robots. “Obviously, this was a big use case at that point of time, in terms of being able to sanitize hospitals and care facilities,” Kunaal Mahanti, physical AI lead at GlobalLogic, told The Robot Report . “So [Haystack ] came up with this concept of being able to do disinfection better.” “While there were disinfections which are happening manually, it wasn’t really good coverage,” he added. “We were really the engineering and collaboration partner there to see how we can take this concept and make it.” The result is an autonomous mobile robot (AMR ) that combines real-time perception, edge-based intelligence, and navigation to deliver hospital-grade UV disinfection with minimal human intervention. The Santa Clara, Calif.-based company said it can operate safety alongside people, interpret its surroundings, and adapt to changes in its environment. GlobalLogic aims to create a scalable platform When designing its robot, Mahanti said GlobalLogic didn’t want to just quickly design a system for one use case or environment. “We wanted to make it an expandable platform,” he explained. “The idea was that you can look at, for example, the track part of it, which is the thing that is carrying the robot, independent of what it is carrying, which is the UV. Architecturally, you keep them separated so that we can mount other things at a later date.” “It went from a concept to what would be an architectural foundation, so that it’s not just that one product,” said Mahanti. “It actually becomes a class of solutions that we can build for the same industry segment.” While GlobalLogic hasn’t done many other deployments in hospitals , Mahanti did say the company used some of the base components of the UV robot for other projects. “When you look at the platform that moves, there are things that have come out from there in terms of the control of the motors,” he said. “Then we use ROS to do the programming and the sensor fusion part, that is reusable, and we’ve used that. So, if not necessarily the same device, but that architecture broadly.” Navigating the challenges that come with hospitals Healthcare facilities are crowded, chaotic, and involve many closed-off spaces, making them difficult for robots to work in. “The known part was that, obviously, you have to interact with humans. The unknown part is that there are doors, there are things that need to be opened, and you can’t always just barge in,” Mahanti said. This is different from more common use cases for mobile robots in warehousing or manufacturing, which typically involve open-spaces that are easy to navigate “There are two modes that we ended up building for [the robots],” noted Mahanti. “Essentially, one was this autonomous mode, where it would navigate and find the right room. The other was a ‘follow me’ mode, in which case it would follow a caregiver or a nurse.” This means the caregiver can open doors and ensure spaces are ready for the robot to enter. It also means a patient wouldn’t be blindsided by a robot entering their room, for example. However, designing an AMR that can work in these complex spaces has created benefits in other parts of GlobalLogic’s business. With a much higher bar for safety, the company could apply the platform to other industries. “The other learning is just being able to be in an environment where you cannot be loud, for example, when we are designing the motors or looking at what we need to put in [the robot],” said Mahanti. “Those things are specific to this industry, but then dealing with that has helped us build machines with higher fidelity elsewhere, where it is not necessarily a given, but it’s a good thing to have. Why wouldn’t you want to have a nice quiet thing that doesn’t interfere with the rest of the environment?” What’s holding back robotic adoption in hospitals? While more robots are making their way into hospitals, most people cannot yet walk into their local hospitals and find robots roaming the halls. This is still an emerging area for robotics, so what challenges still exist? Mahanti said three things come to mind. The first is cost. “There needs to be an ROI,” he replied. “For example, if you look at this use case during COVID, at that point of time, you needed less people in the hospitals. You needed to be safe. It was a big issue. So that ROI was justifiable.” Second is compliance with medical standards , which becomes much trickier when deploying robots that will interact with the public and patients. Third is the perception of robots. Mahanti acknowledged that hospital staffers don’t want a big, bulky robot taking up space in busy corridors and elevators. Prem Balasubramanian, chief technology officer of GlobalLogic, said that safely integrating into hospital workflows is also challenging. “There are clearly safety concerns, from multiple angles. Navigating in a very human-crowded situation is not easy,” he said. “For a disinfectant use case, if a robot waits for people to keep moving and then slowly moves, you’re okay. But if you’re using it for anything else, like if a doctor calls and you have to get something fast to help a patient or bring some stuff, a robot could get stuck because it sees people moving and it can’t move.” The hospital is difficult on its own, and it’s made even more difficult when you consider how made-for-humans they are, said Balasubramanian. For example, a robot might be able to navigate an emergency room in a perfect condition with no obstacles, but the addition of patients who constantly moving or being moved and staffers running around to solve critical issues make navigation much more challenging. “The entire workflow within a hospital is built for humans. You can’t just fit a robot in thinking it’s a human. So, there is work to be done in converting some of the workflow, the spaces, everything,” Balasubramanian said. Submit your innovation now! selectedItems.title: LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action
selectedItems.summary: LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation. The post LiberAI Unveils Liber-0, a World Action Model That Grounds Human Experience in Robot Action appeared first on The Robot Report .
selectedItems.articleText: LiberAI introduces Liber-0, a world action model pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience to support zero-shot robot manipulation. In an evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6, it achieved 36.0% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those target tasks. The model combines large-scale human video, glove-recorded hand motion and embodiment alignment to transfer human manipulation experience to robots. Liber-0 achieves 36.0% overall success in a zero-shot evaluation of 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6. LiberAI has introduced Liber-0, a world action model (WAM) pretrained on more than 2.2 million hours of human experience. The Beijing-based startup said the model combines human video with glove-recorded motion and embodiment-conditioned learning to transfer human manipulation experience to robots. A central test of Liber-0’s generalization is whether it can perform target tasks without robot demonstrations collected specifically for them. LiberAI evaluated the model on a separate suite of 60 GPT-6-proposed tasks, distinct from its internal scaling benchmarks: 20 pick-and-place (PnP) tasks, 20 non-PnP manipulation tasks, and 20 challenging non-PnP and long-horizon tasks. Examples from the suite include placing a pen in a pencil case, pushing a drawer closed, and a longer sequence in which a pen is placed in a pouch and the pouch is stored in a drawer. LiberAI reported task success rates of 63.5% on pick-and-place tasks, 34.0% on non-pick-and-place manipulation tasks and 10.5% on challenging non-pick-and-place and long-horizon tasks, with an overall success rate of 36.0% across 600 trials. Here, zero-shot means the evaluated checkpoint was not trained on robot demonstrations collected specifically for these target tasks; pretraining still included robot data. Why learn from people? Robot manipulation has traditionally relied heavily on demonstrations recorded on a specific robot for a specific task, usually by a human operator teleoperating the machine. That data closely matches deployment, but collecting it can be slow and expensive, particularly when new tasks or robot platforms require additional demonstrations. Human activity is far more abundant, and much of it is already on video. The obstacle, according to LiberAI, is that human video does not translate directly into robot commands. Cameras sit in different places, hand poses estimated from video are noisy, and human bodies move differently from robots. Liber-0 connects human experience with robot action in three ways. First, LiberSense Glove, LiberAI’s data-collection system, directly records hand movements, helping link human video to the motions behind it. Second, LiberAI’s robot platform uses camera views and hand, wrist and waist movements that more closely match those of humans, making skills easier to transfer. Third, a Unified Embodiment Representation gives the model information about body shape and joint movement, so it can adapt actions to the body performing them. Liber-0 jointly predicts future video frames and actions. This lets it learn from ordinary videos without action labels alongside glove and robot recordings that include measured motion. Human-to-robot transfer. Conceptual illustration of how action-grounded human recordings and visual and kinematic alignment support transfer to LEO. Learning actions that robot data lacked Glove data can also introduce behaviors missing from a policy’s robot data. LiberAI trained policies whose robot demonstrations covered only pick-and-place, while glove demonstrations included actions such as folding, pressing and opening. Performance was measured as a progress score, a 0 to 100 measure that credits partial completion, across four pick-and-place and six non-PnP tasks. With robot data alone, the non-PnP progress score was 2.2. Adding glove recordings of those actions raised it to 47.5, and to 54.6 when the glove set also included pick-and-place, close to the 56.3 scored by a policy trained on robot demonstrations of every action. This controlled experiment is separate from the 60-task suite: the actions appeared in the glove demonstrations but not in the policies’ robot demonstrations. A quarter of the robot data A separate experiment examines whether glove recordings can reduce the need for robot demonstrations. In an eight-task evaluation on LiberAI’s robot platform, where the full robot and glove pools contained equal numbers of demonstrations, a policy trained on 25% of the robot pool plus 100% of the glove pool reached a progress score of 75.6. A policy trained on 100% of the robot pool scored 72.8. In that setting, glove recordings delivered comparable performance with 75% fewer robot demonstrations. The saving applies to robot demonstrations specifically, as the mixed policy still drew on the full glove pool. Because glove collection does not require a robot at each site, LiberAI says experience can be gathered from more people, in more places, and potentially at lower cost. Evaluating the pretrained model directly On LiberAI’s internal benchmarks, the pretrained checkpoint achieved progress scores of 81.4 on pick-and-place and 72.3 on non-PnP tasks when evaluated directly. Robot post-training added 2.2 and 1.5 points, to 83.6 and 73.8. LiberAI said the small gain indicates the pretrained model already captures much of the capability needed for the evaluated tasks. LiberAI has developed an interactive simulation in which users can upload their own objects and watch Liber-0 manipulate them in a virtual environment. The simulation demonstrates object-level generalization: that version of the model was post-trained on 100 hours of simulated teleoperation data and receives no further object-specific training. “Human video shows what people do, but not exactly how their hands move or how that movement fits a different body,” said Songming Liu, founder and CEO of LiberAI. “Grounding that experience in measured motion and aligning it with the robot’s body is what turns it into robot capability.” Introducing Liber-0, our World Action Model for zero-shot robot manipulation—including dexterous, multi-step tasks. Across 60 tasks proposed by GPT-6 and 600 trials, Liber-0 achieved 36% overall success without robot demonstrations collected specifically for those tasks: • Pick-and-place: 63.5% • Other manipulation tasks: 34.0% • Challenging multi-step tasks: 10.5% Zero-shot capability extends beyond individual actions to coordinated sequences. Pretrained on 2.2M+ hours of human experience, Liber-0 jointly predicts future observations and actions to turn human experience into robot skills. Technical blog: https://t.co/X5NMTjsr8r — LiberAI (@liberai_robot) November 4, 2026 What’s next for LiberAI LiberAI noted that LiberSense Glove currently records hand poses and trajectories but not contact or force, which matter for insertion, fastening and handling soft materials. Tactile and force sensing, alongside data collection across a wider range of homes, remain future research directions. Watch Liber-0 in action and explore the full evaluation on LiberAI .
